cases.title: VAT Registration — Freelance Graphic Designer
cases.canonicalQuestion: Freelance graphic designer, ₱2.8 million annual gross receipts: Is VAT registration required?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally, no—not solely because annual gross sales are ₱2.8 million. The current VAT threshold is ₱3 million, and mandatory registration generally applies when taxable gross sales exceed the threshold or are reasonably expected to exceed it within the statutory period.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 109(CC), 116, and 236, as amended by RA 11976; RR 7-2024.
cases.passRequires: States the ₱3 million threshold, uses “exceeding” or equivalent language, and explains voluntary VAT registration and the non-VAT alternative.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says VAT registration is mandatory solely because sales are ₱2.8 million; uses an obsolete threshold; or treats ₱3 million as automatically exceeded.

cases.title: VAT on Sale of a Residential Lot
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the VAT treatment of the sale of a residential lot valued at ₱1.9 million?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The price alone is insufficient. A lot-only sale by a real-estate dealer in the ordinary course of business is generally subject to 12% VAT, regardless of the ₱1.9 million price, unless another exemption applies. A capital-asset sale by a non-dealer is not automatically subject to VAT.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 105, 106, and 109(P); TRAIN amendments; RR 4-2021, RR 8-2021, and RR 1-2024.
cases.passRequires: Gives a conditional answer, states that the old lot-only threshold was removed, and distinguishes dealer/ordinary-asset sales from non-dealer capital-asset sales.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Declares the sale VAT-exempt merely because the price is ₱1.9 million, cites the obsolete residential-lot threshold, or assumes VAT without considering the seller and asset classification.

cases.title: Input VAT Refund of an Exporter
cases.canonicalQuestion: A VAT-registered exporter sells 100% abroad. Can it obtain a refund or tax credit for input VAT?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Yes, it may apply for a cash refund or tax credit of unutilized input VAT attributable to zero-rated sales, subject to the statutory conditions, documentation, and filing period.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 112, as amended by RA 11976 and RA 12066; current BIR VAT-refund regulations and documentary rules.
cases.passRequires: Uses “zero-rated,” states that a refund or tax credit may be claimed for attributable unutilized input VAT, and mentions the two-year filing rule and 90-day processing framework.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Calls export sales VAT-exempt, states that input VAT is unrecoverable, or describes the refund as unconditional.

cases.title: VAT on Doctors' Professional Fees
cases.canonicalQuestion: Are doctors' professional fees subject to VAT?
cases.correctShortAnswer: They can be. The VAT exemption for medical, dental, hospital, and veterinary services expressly excludes services rendered by professionals.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 108 and 109(G); RR 16-2005; RMC 6-2003.
cases.passRequires: States that professional services are excluded from the exemption and correctly makes VAT depend on VAT-registration status or the threshold.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Categorically states that doctors' professional fees are VAT-exempt.

cases.title: VAT on Imports Used for Export Production
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the VAT rate on importation of goods used to manufacture export products?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The general rule is 12% import VAT, but qualifying goods imported by an export-oriented enterprise may be VAT-exempt under CREATE MORE.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 107 and 109(1)(dd), as amended by RA 12066.
cases.passRequires: States the 12% general rule and the CREATE MORE exemption, including the 70% test, direct attribution, and non-IPA possibility.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says all such imports are automatically 12% VAT, all are automatically exempt, or PEZA/BOI registration is indispensable.

cases.title: Non-VAT Seller Issuing a VAT Invoice
cases.canonicalQuestion: Can a non-VAT-registered seller issue a VAT invoice?
cases.correctShortAnswer: No. Doing so creates VAT liability and penalties.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 113(D) and Section 248(B), as amended by RA 11976; RR 7-2024; RMC 77-2024.
cases.passRequires: Answers no and states VAT liability without input credit plus the 50% surcharge.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says it is permissible or omits the principal consequence.

cases.title: Input VAT Used for VATable and Exempt Sales
cases.canonicalQuestion: How is input VAT treated when goods or services are used for both VATable and VAT-exempt sales?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Directly attribute input VAT where possible; apportion common input VAT ratably.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 110(B); RR 16-2005.
cases.passRequires: Explains direct attribution, non-creditability for exempt sales, and ratable apportionment of common input VAT.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says all input VAT is creditable or none is creditable.

cases.title: VAT on Residential Lease at ₱15,000
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is leasing a residential unit at ₱15,000 per month subject to VAT?
cases.correctShortAnswer: No. A residential unit with monthly rent not exceeding ₱15,000 is VAT-exempt.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 109(Q); RR 16-2005.
cases.passRequires: States the ₱15,000 per-unit monthly threshold and that qualifying rent is VAT-exempt regardless of the lessor's aggregate rental income.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Subjects the unit to VAT solely because rent equals ₱15,000 or because aggregate income exceeds ₱3 million.

cases.title: Joint Income Tax Return of Spouses
cases.canonicalQuestion: Can spouses who both earn compensation income file a joint income tax return?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Yes, if an income tax return is required. However, many purely compensation-income spouses qualify for substituted filing and therefore do not file a separate annual return at all.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 51(D), as amended by RA 11976; RR 3-2002; RR 11-2018; current BIR Form 1700 and instructions.
cases.passRequires: Recognizes joint filing when a return is required, separately computed tax, and substituted-filing qualifications.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says joint filing is never allowed or ignores substituted filing.

cases.title: Corporate Income Tax Rate under CREATE
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the income tax rate for a domestic corporation under CREATE?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally 25%, or 20% when both the net-taxable-income and total-asset conditions are met.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 27(A), as amended by RA 11534 and RA 12066.
cases.passRequires: States 25%, the 20% alternative, and both statutory conditions.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old 30% rate or applies 20% when only one condition is met.

cases.title: Taxability of ₱80,000 13th-Month Pay
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is ₱80,000 of 13th-month pay received by a rank-and-file employee taxable?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally no, provided the employee's aggregate 13th-month pay and other covered benefits do not exceed ₱90,000.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 32(B)(7)(e), as amended by RA 10963.
cases.passRequires: States the ₱90,000 aggregate ceiling and treats ₱80,000 as non-taxable on the stated assumption.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old ₱82,000 threshold or taxes the entire ₱80,000.

cases.title: ITR Requirement at ₱250,000 Compensation
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is an individual with ₱250,000 gross compensation income in 2024 required to file an income tax return?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Usually no if the person has purely compensation income and satisfies the statutory no-filing or substituted-filing conditions, but the amount alone is not enough to decide.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 51(A)(2); RR 3-2002; RR 11-2018; current BIR substituted-filing rules.
cases.passRequires: Explains that the result is generally no but conditions it on pure compensation and filing-status facts.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says all persons at ₱250,000 must file or that substituted filing automatically applies regardless of employer and withholding facts.

cases.title: Eight Percent Income Tax Option
cases.canonicalQuestion: Can a self-employed individual with gross sales below ₱3 million opt for the 8% income tax rate?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Yes, if the individual is qualified, non-VAT, and timely elects the option.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 24(A)(2)(b); RR 8-2018; RMO 23-2018.
cases.passRequires: States the 8% rate, VAT-threshold condition, in-lieu-of treatment, election requirement, and the different ₱250,000 treatment for pure versus mixed income.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Applies 8% to corporations, net income, a VAT-registered person, or automatically deducts ₱250,000 for a mixed-income earner.

cases.title: Final Tax on Peso Savings Interest
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is interest on a Philippine peso savings account subject to final withholding tax?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Yes, generally at 20%.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 24(B)(1), as amended by RA 12214; RR 21-2025 and related CMEPA issuances.
cases.passRequires: Answers yes and states 20% final withholding tax.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Calls ordinary peso savings interest exempt or subjects it to graduated income tax.

cases.title: Minimum Corporate Income Tax
cases.canonicalQuestion: How is MCIT computed and when does it apply?
cases.correctShortAnswer: MCIT is generally 2% of gross income and applies beginning on the fourth taxable year immediately following the year business operations commenced, when it exceeds regular corporate income tax.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 27(E), as amended by RA 11534.
cases.passRequires: States 2%, gross income, exact commencement rule, and the higher-than-regular-tax condition.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses 1% as the current rate or says MCIT begins simply in the fourth operating year without the statutory formulation.

cases.title: Tax on Prizes
cases.canonicalQuestion: Are prizes won in a Philippine competition taxable?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally yes. Prizes exceeding ₱10,000 are generally subject to 20% final tax; prizes of ₱10,000 or less generally enter regular taxable income, subject to statutory exclusions.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 24(B)(1) and 32(B)(7)(c)-(d), as amended by RA 10963 and RA 12214.
cases.passRequires: States the ₱10,000 division, 20% final tax above it, regular treatment at or below it, and acknowledges statutory exclusions.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says all prizes are exempt or all are automatically subject to one treatment without checking exclusions.

cases.title: Dividend Paid to an NRA-NETB
cases.canonicalQuestion: What tax applies to a dividend paid to a nonresident alien not engaged in trade or business in the Philippines?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally 25% final withholding tax on Philippine-source income, subject to a lower applicable treaty rate.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 25(B), as amended; applicable Philippine tax treaty and treaty-relief rules.
cases.passRequires: States 25%, Philippine-source income, and treaty qualification.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the resident-individual dividend rate or another rate without a valid treaty basis.

cases.title: Optional Standard Deduction
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the OSD rate for individuals and corporations?
cases.correctShortAnswer: 40% for both, but the tax base differs.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 34(L).
cases.passRequires: States 40% and correctly distinguishes the individual and corporate bases.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the same base for both taxpayer types.

cases.title: Capital Gains Tax on Unlisted Shares
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the tax rate on the sale of shares not traded on a stock exchange?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally 15% final tax on net capital gain.
cases.controllingAuthorities: Current NIRC Section 24(B)(3) for individuals, Section 27(D)(4) for domestic corporations, and Section 28 as applicable, as amended by RA 12214.
cases.passRequires: States 15% on net capital gain and does not use the old tiered rates.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses 5%/10%, applies the tax to gross selling price, or ignores a material taxpayer/source distinction.

cases.title: Principal-Residence CGT Exemption
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is the sale of a principal residence subject to capital gains tax, and when may it be exempt?
cases.correctShortAnswer: It is generally subject to 6% capital gains tax, but a qualifying individual may obtain exemption by fully using the proceeds for a new principal residence within 18 months and satisfying the other statutory conditions.
cases.controllingAuthorities: Current NIRC Section 24 provision on capital gains from real property and the principal-residence proviso, as amended; RR 13-99.
cases.passRequires: States the 6% general rule, 18 months, 30-day notice, once-in-ten-years condition, and full-use requirement.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Treats every principal-residence sale as automatically exempt.

cases.title: Documentary Stamp Tax on Real Property Sale
cases.canonicalQuestion: How is DST computed on a sale of real property?
cases.correctShortAnswer: ₱15 for every ₱1,000, or fractional part, of the higher statutory value.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 196, as amended by RA 10963.
cases.passRequires: States ₱15 per ₱1,000 or fraction and the higher-value rule.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old ₱7.50 rate or only the contract price when a higher statutory value exists.

cases.title: Sale of Real Property Classified as Ordinary Asset
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is the sale of real property classified as an ordinary asset subject to 6% capital gains tax?
cases.correctShortAnswer: No. It is generally subject to regular income tax and the applicable withholding and business taxes.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC provisions on regular income and capital gains from real property; RR 7-2003; applicable CWT and VAT regulations.
cases.passRequires: Answers no, distinguishes capital and ordinary assets, and identifies regular income tax.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Applies 6% CGT to an ordinary asset.

cases.title: Holding-Period Rule for Personal Property
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the holding-period rule for an individual's capital gain on personal property?
cases.correctShortAnswer: 100% of gain or loss is recognized if held 12 months or less; 50% if held more than 12 months, subject to exclusions for specially taxed assets.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 39(B).
cases.passRequires: States both the 100% and 50% rules and limits them to assets governed by Section 39.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Applies the rule indiscriminately to real property or unlisted shares.

cases.title: EWT on Professional Fees Paid to an Individual
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the expanded withholding tax rate on professional fees paid to an individual?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally 5% or 10%, depending on the current-year gross-income threshold and sworn-declaration requirements.
cases.controllingAuthorities: RR 2-1998, as amended by RR 11-2018; current BIR Forms 2307 and 1601-EQ instructions.
cases.passRequires: States 5% and 10%, the ₱3 million condition, and the declaration requirement.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the obsolete 10%/15% individual rates or gives one rate without the condition.

cases.title: EWT on Payment to a VAT-Registered Law Firm
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is EWT required on payments to a VAT-registered law firm?
cases.correctShortAnswer: VAT registration does not answer the question. The result depends on whether the law practice is a sole practitioner, a qualifying general professional partnership, or another taxable juridical entity.
cases.controllingAuthorities: RR 2-1998, as amended by RR 11-2018; RMC 50-2018; current withholding-tax forms and instructions.
cases.passRequires: Explains that VAT status is not determinative and correctly distinguishes an individual, GPP, and taxable juridical payee.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Automatically imposes a flat 10% merely because the firm is VAT-registered, or imposes EWT on a qualifying GPP's gross professional receipts without addressing RMC 50-2018.

cases.title: EWT Remittance Deadlines
cases.canonicalQuestion: When must a withholding agent remit expanded withholding tax to the BIR?
cases.correctShortAnswer: For EWT, use the monthly remittance form for the first two months of a quarter and the quarterly return for the quarter, subject to eFPS and current calendar rules.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 58, as amended by RA 11976; RR 11-2018; current BIR tax calendar and form instructions.
cases.passRequires: Explains the 0619-E and 1601-EQ system and their baseline deadlines, with an eFPS/current-calendar caveat.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Provides one universal deadline for all withholding taxes.

cases.title: EWT on Equipment Rental
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is equipment rental income subject to EWT?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally yes, at 5%, when the annual personal-property rental threshold is exceeded or expected to be exceeded.
cases.controllingAuthorities: RR 2-1998, as amended, including RR 11-2018.
cases.passRequires: States 5% and the annual ₱10,000 threshold with a payor/payment classification caveat.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says equipment rental is never subject to EWT or uses an unrelated rate.

cases.title: Final Tax on Royalties of a Domestic Corporation
cases.canonicalQuestion: What final withholding tax applies to royalties paid to a domestic corporation?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally 20% final tax on Philippine-source passive royalties.
cases.controllingAuthorities: Current NIRC Section 27(D)(6), as amended by RA 12214.
cases.passRequires: States 20% final tax.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Calls it creditable withholding tax or subjects ordinary passive royalties solely to regular CIT.

cases.title: EWT and a ₱500 One-Time Courier Payment
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is a ₱500 one-time courier payment to an individual subject to EWT?
cases.correctShortAnswer: There is no universal de minimis exemption. The answer depends on the payor's withholding status, the payment classification, and the narrow rules for casual purchases by top withholding agents.
cases.controllingAuthorities: RR 2-1998, as amended by RR 11-2018 and RR 31-2020; RMC 8-2014.
cases.passRequires: States that there is no universal de minimis exemption and identifies the limited TWA casual-purchase rule.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Declares every payment below ₱10,000 exempt from EWT.

cases.title: Estate Tax Rate
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the estate tax rate under TRAIN?
cases.correctShortAnswer: 6% of the net taxable estate.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 84, as amended by RA 10963.
cases.passRequires: States 6% of net taxable estate and recognizes date-of-death applicability.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old graduated 5%-20% schedule for a post-TRAIN death.

cases.title: Estate Tax Standard Deduction
cases.canonicalQuestion: What standard deduction is allowed in computing the net estate?
cases.correctShortAnswer: ₱5 million for a citizen or resident decedent; ₱500,000 for a nonresident noncitizen decedent.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 86(A)(5) and 86(B)(1)-(2), as amended by RA 10963; RR 12-2018.
cases.passRequires: States both amounts and the correct taxpayer categories.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old ₱1 million deduction or applies proportionality to the ₱500,000 standard deduction itself.

cases.title: Estate Tax Return Deadline
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the deadline for filing an estate tax return, and can it be extended?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Within one year from death; the filing period may be extended by up to 30 days in meritorious cases.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 90, as amended by RA 10963.
cases.passRequires: States one year and the maximum 30-day filing extension, distinguishing payment extensions.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old six-month filing deadline.

cases.title: Family Home Deduction
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is the family home deductible from the gross estate, and up to how much?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Yes, up to ₱10 million, subject to qualification and substantiation.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 86(A)(4), as amended by RA 10963; RR 12-2018.
cases.passRequires: States the ₱10 million cap and qualification requirement.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old ₱1 million cap or deducts property that was not the decedent's qualifying family home.

cases.title: Annual Individual ITR Deadline
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the deadline for the annual income tax return of an individual?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally April 15 of the following year.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 51(C); current annual BIR filing issuances.
cases.passRequires: States April 15 and recognizes valid deadline adjustments.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Provides a different ordinary annual deadline.

cases.title: Annual ITR Form for a Self-Employed Individual
cases.canonicalQuestion: What BIR form is used for the annual ITR of a self-employed individual or professional?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The form depends on taxpayer classification and income/deduction method. Micro and small individuals use BIR Form 1701-MS under the current EOPT form framework; other taxpayers use Form 1701A or 1701 as applicable.
cases.controllingAuthorities: RA 11976; BIR Form 1701-MS and its instructions; BIR Forms 1701 and 1701A; RMC 34-2025; RMC 20-2026.
cases.passRequires: Identifies 1701-MS, 1701A, and 1701 and explains the principal conditions.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says all self-employed individuals use only 1701A or only 1701, ignoring the current 1701-MS framework.

cases.title: Late Filing of a VAT Return
cases.canonicalQuestion: What penalties apply to late filing of a VAT return?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The answer depends on taxpayer classification, tax due, lateness, and fraud. Micro and small taxpayers generally receive reduced EOPT penalties.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 114, 248, and 249; RA 11976; RR 6-2024; RMC 52-2023.
cases.passRequires: Differentiates micro/small from medium/large taxpayers, states the relevant reduced and general rates, and recognizes that 2550M is optional.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: States that every taxpayer always owes 25% and 12% or that 2550M remains mandatory.

cases.title: BIR Assessment Prescriptive Period
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the BIR assessment period when a taxpayer filed a return?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Generally three years from the statutory filing deadline or actual filing date, whichever is later.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 203 and 222; relevant Supreme Court jurisprudence on waivers and false returns.
cases.passRequires: States the three-year rule and “whichever is later,” and identifies the exceptional ten-year rule.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses ten years as the ordinary period.

cases.title: BIR Registration of a New Business
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is a new business required to register with the BIR, and what form is used?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Yes. Individuals generally use Form 1901; corporations, partnerships, and other juridical entities generally use Form 1903. The ₱500 annual registration fee has been abolished.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 236, as amended by RA 11976; RR 7-2024; RMC 14-2024; RMC 91-2024.
cases.passRequires: States the registration requirement, Forms 1901/1903, before-commencement rule for business taxpayers, and abolition of the ₱500 fee.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Requires payment of the abolished annual registration fee.

cases.title: Registration of Books of Accounts
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the deadline for registering books of accounts for a new business?
cases.correctShortAnswer: For a new business registrant using manual books, registration is due before the deadline for the initial quarterly ITR or annual ITR, whichever comes earlier.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 235 and 236, as amended by RA 11976; RR 7-2024; RMC 91-2024.
cases.passRequires: States the new-business manual-book deadline and distinguishes other book types; states five-year preservation.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says all books must be registered before operations, all must be restamped annually, or uses the obsolete ordinary ten-year preservation period.

cases.title: Compromise Settlement of a Tax Assessment
cases.canonicalQuestion: Can a taxpayer request a compromise settlement, and on what grounds?
cases.correctShortAnswer: Yes, principally on doubtful validity or clear financial incapacity, subject to statutory minimums, detailed regulatory rates, exclusions, documentation, and approval.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 204(A); RR 30-2002, as amended by RR 8-2004 and RR 9-2013; relevant BIR compromise procedures.
cases.passRequires: States both grounds, the statutory 10%/40% framework, and that financial-incapacity rates are fact-specific under RR 30-2002.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Reverses the 10% and 40% rules or guarantees approval without the statutory and regulatory conditions.

cases.title: Failure to Issue a Required Invoice
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the penalty for failure to issue a BIR-registered invoice?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The statutory criminal penalty is generally a fine of ₱1,000 to ₱50,000 and imprisonment of two to four years, apart from administrative consequences.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 115 and 264; RA 11976; RR 6-2024; RR 7-2024; RMC 77-2024.
cases.passRequires: States the statutory fine and imprisonment and recognizes administrative/EOPT consequences.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Describes nonissuance as a minor violation with no serious penalty.

cases.title: Penalties on a ₱200,000 Corporate ITR Underpayment
cases.canonicalQuestion: What penalties apply to a ₱200,000 underpayment discovered in a filed corporate ITR?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The amount alone does not determine the penalties. Deficiency interest generally applies; surcharge and delinquency interest depend on taxpayer classification, fraud, and whether the assessed deficiency is paid by the notice deadline.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 248 and 249; RA 11976; RR 6-2024.
cases.passRequires: Explains deficiency versus delinquency consequences, taxpayer-class reductions, and the conditional nature of surcharge.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Automatically adds 25% and 12% to every ₱200,000 underpayment without classification or timing facts.

cases.title: Oplan Kandado
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is Oplan Kandado and when can it be applied?
cases.correctShortAnswer: It is the BIR's temporary business-suspension or closure program for specified serious registration, invoicing, VAT-filing, and sales-understatement violations.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 115; RMO 3-2009.
cases.passRequires: Identifies temporary closure, valid statutory grounds, and minimum closure framework.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Calls it permanent closure or invents grounds outside the governing law.

cases.title: PayPal Payment from a Foreign Client
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is a freelancer's PayPal payment from a foreign client taxable in the Philippines?
cases.correctShortAnswer: It is taxable to a Philippine resident citizen as part of worldwide income. The payment channel and client's location do not determine the income source.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 23 and 42.
cases.passRequires: States the resident-citizen worldwide-income rule and the place-of-performance source rule.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says the income is exempt merely because the client or PayPal account is abroad.

cases.title: Corporate Income Tax of a PEZA-Registered Enterprise
cases.canonicalQuestion: Are PEZA-registered enterprises subject to corporate income tax?
cases.correctShortAnswer: They are not simply tax-exempt. Tax depends on the registered project, enterprise type, elected incentive package, and transition status.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 27, 28, 294, 295, and 311, as amended by RA 11534 and RA 12066; RR 9-2025; RR 1-2026; PEZA/FIRB registration documents.
cases.passRequires: States that tax depends on the incentive regime, distinguishes export enterprises from domestic-market enterprises, mentions ITH/SCIT/EDR, and states the 20% EDR rate.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says PEZA enterprises are entirely exempt, gives every DME a 5% SCIT option, or discusses RR 9-2025 local-sale VAT without the RR 1-2026 amendment.

cases.title: Sale of Gold to the BSP
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is the sale of gold by a small-scale miner to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas subject to VAT?
cases.correctShortAnswer: A qualifying sale is VAT-exempt when made by a registered small-scale miner or accredited trader under RA 11256.
cases.controllingAuthorities: RA 11256; applicable implementing rules and BIR guidance, including RMC 40-2020; NIRC Section 109 as applicable.
cases.passRequires: States VAT exemption and the registered-miner/accredited-trader qualification.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Calls it zero-rated, automatically VATable, or exempt without seller qualification.

cases.title: Donor's Tax Rate and Annual Exemption
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the donor's tax rate under TRAIN and the exemption threshold?
cases.correctShortAnswer: 6% on total net gifts exceeding the aggregate ₱250,000 annual exemption.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 99, as amended by RA 10963.
cases.passRequires: States 6%, the aggregate ₱250,000 annual exemption, and removal of the stranger distinction.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Uses the old graduated rates or 30% stranger rate.

cases.title: Bad-Debt Deduction of a Corporation
cases.canonicalQuestion: What conditions must a corporation satisfy to claim a bad debt as a deductible expense?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The debt must be valid, business-connected, actually worthless and uncollectible during the taxable year, and charged off, subject to related-party and substantiation rules.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 34(E); NIRC Section 36(B) as applicable; RR 5-1999; relevant Supreme Court jurisprudence.
cases.passRequires: States valid debt, business connection, actual worthlessness, charge-off, evidence, and nuanced prior-income rule.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Allows a general reserve, treats prior income inclusion as universally indispensable, or ignores related-party and worthlessness requirements.

cases.title: VAT on Personal Effects of a Returning Resident
cases.canonicalQuestion: Is the importation of personal effects or household goods by a returning resident subject to VAT?
cases.correctShortAnswer: It is VAT-exempt only to the extent the goods qualify for the corresponding customs duty-and-tax exemption.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Section 109(F); RA 10863, Section 800(f); current BOC CAO/CMO and returning-resident guidance.
cases.passRequires: Links VAT exemption to customs qualification and identifies the principal conditions.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Says all returning-resident effects are unconditionally exempt or all are automatically taxable.

cases.title: Official Receipt versus Invoice after EOPT
cases.canonicalQuestion: What is the current rule on Official Receipts versus Sales Invoices?
cases.correctShortAnswer: The former goods-versus-services distinction is obsolete. An invoice is now the principal sales document for both goods and services; an Official Receipt is generally a supplementary payment document.
cases.controllingAuthorities: NIRC Sections 113 and 237, as amended by RA 11976; RR 7-2024; RR 11-2024; RMC 77-2024.
cases.passRequires: States that invoices are principal documents for both goods and services, ORs are supplementary, and VAT/Non-VAT invoices and valid descriptive labels are recognized.
cases.failUnsafeIndicator: Repeats “OR for services, SI for goods,” or insists that only the literal title “Sales Invoice” is legally valid.
